title: What Is Zardozi Work? How to Spot It and Style a Zardozi Anarkali
excerpt: Zardozi is hand embroidery in metallic thread, beads and sequins. Learn how to tell real hand zardozi from machine work, and how to style a zardozi Anarkali for weddings.
body:
Zardozi is a traditional Indian hand embroidery done with metallic thread, beads, sequins and small metal wires called dabka. It sits slightly raised on the fabric and catches the light, which is why it is a favourite for wedding and festive wear. On an Anarkali, it is usually placed on the neckline, yoke and sleeve cuffs, so the face and hands are framed in soft gold.

*By the Bahe Kurtiz team, Jaipur. Our handwork is done by karigars in our own Jaipur unit.*

**Quick answer**

- Zardozi = hand embroidery with metallic thread, dabka, beads and sequins
- Real hand zardozi is slightly raised and a little uneven, in a good way
- Machine work is flat, perfectly repeated and usually on the whole fabric
- On an Anarkali, zardozi on the yoke and cuffs keeps the look elegant, not heavy
- Dry clean only, and store with tissue over the embroidery

## Where does zardozi come from?

The word comes from Persian: *zar* means gold and *dozi* means embroidery. The craft grew in the Mughal courts, where it was worked with real gold and silver wire. Today most zardozi uses metallic-finish thread and dabka, which keeps the same look at a price you can actually wear to a friend's wedding.

Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra and Bareilly are well-known centres for the craft. In Jaipur, it is often paired with gota work, the flat metallic ribbon used on hems and dupatta borders.

## How can I tell hand zardozi from machine embroidery?

| Check | Hand zardozi | Machine embroidery |
|---|---|---|
| Feel | Raised, textured, you can feel the dabka coils | Flat and smooth |
| Pattern | Tiny variations between motifs | Every motif exactly the same |
| Back side | Visible knots and stitches, often covered with a lining | Neat thread mesh |
| Materials | Dabka, beads, sequins, cutdana mixed together | Mostly thread only |
| Placement | Focused areas: neckline, yoke, cuffs | Often spread over the whole fabric |

Small differences between the left and right sleeve cuff are normal in handwork. They are a sign that a person, not a machine, made your piece.

## Why does zardozi look so good on an Anarkali?

An Anarkali has a fitted bodice and a full, flowing skirt. Zardozi on the neckline and yoke draws the eye up to the face, while the plain flare keeps the outfit light and easy to move in. Add gota lace on the hem and the outfit shines at both ends without feeling heavy.

Our [Ruhani lavender georgette Anarkali](/products/lavender-georgette-anarkali-suit-zardozi-handwork-gota-lace-dupatta/) is a good example. The V-neckline and sleeve cuffs are worked by hand in pure zardozi, with a matching motif at the centre of the yoke, while the georgette flare is finished with layered gota lace. A cotton lining keeps it comfortable through a long evening.

## How do I style a zardozi Anarkali?

### For a sangeet or mehendi

Go playful. Pearl chandbalis, a small bindi and soft open curls work beautifully with a pastel like lavender. Drape the dupatta over one arm so it flows when you dance. Nude block heels or juttis are easier than stilettos on grass or a dance floor.

### For a wedding or reception

Pin the dupatta on both shoulders so the gota border frames the outfit. Choose earrings in the same gold tone as the zardozi. Antique gold or kundan works better than bright yellow gold. Keep the neck bare so the embroidered neckline is the focus.

### For a winter event abroad

Add a long camel or cream coat over the Anarkali and change into heels indoors. Pearls and a soft pink lip keep the look light. Our guide to [layering Indian outfits in winter](/blog/how-to-layer-indian-outfits-in-winter-abroad/) has more ideas.

> **From our Jaipur studio:** Zardozi motifs are stitched on a frame called an *adda*, one small section at a time. A neckline and two cuffs can take a karigar a full day or more, which is why handwork pieces take a little longer to make.

## How do I care for zardozi?

- Dry clean only. Water can dull the metallic thread.
- Store folded in a muslin or cotton cloth, with tissue paper over the embroidery so it does not snag.
- Iron on low heat on the reverse side, never directly on the zardozi.
- Keep perfume and deodorant away from the embroidery.

For the georgette itself, see [how to care for a georgette Anarkali](/blog/how-to-care-for-a-georgette-anarkali/).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is zardozi made with real gold?**
Traditionally it was. Today most zardozi, including ours, uses metallic-finish thread and dabka, which gives the same look and is far more affordable.

**Is zardozi heavy to wear?**
Not when it is placed on the neckline, yoke and cuffs. The rest of the Anarkali stays light.

**Can I wash a zardozi Anarkali at home?**
We do not recommend it. Dry cleaning keeps the metallic thread bright and the shape of the embroidery intact.

**What is the difference between zardozi and gota work?**
Zardozi is embroidery made of thread, dabka, beads and sequins. Gota is a flat metallic ribbon stitched onto the fabric, usually on hems and borders.
